contradictions.question: Should you serve God alone?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 4:10 quotes Deuteronomy 6:13 and tells Satan that one should worship and serve God *only* — and Matthew 23:10 says no one but Christ should be called *kathēgētēs* (master/teacher). Then the household codes in Ephesians 6:5, Colossians 3:22, 1 Timothy 6:1, Titus 2:9, and 1 Peter 2:18 instruct slaves to obey their human masters in everything. The same canon that demands exclusive service to God also institutionalizes obedience to human masters.
contradictions.commentary:
The tension here turns on the Greek vocabulary, and the apologist harmonization actually does some legitimate lexical work — but it doesn't survive the household codes intact.

Matthew 4:10 (citing Deut 6:13 LXX) uses *latreuseis* — cultic worship-service, the kind of devotion owed to a deity. Matthew 23:10's *kathēgētēs* is teacher/guide in a religious authority sense. The household codes use *hypotassō* (be subject) and *hypakouō* (obey) toward *kyrioi* (masters) in the social-economic slave-relationship sense. Different Greek words, different conceptual fields.

The standard apologist move — Blomberg, Carson, the IVP *Hard Sayings* crew — is that *latreuō* (cultic service) and *douleuō*/*hypakouō* (domestic obedience) are separate categories. Render unto Caesar, etc. Fair enough on the lexicography.

But here's where it falls apart. 1 Peter 2:18 tells slaves to be subject to their masters *en panti phobō* — 'with all fear' — the same *phobos* the New Testament reserves elsewhere for reverence of God (1 Pet 2:17 in the same paragraph: *ton theon phobeisthe*). Colossians 3:22 tells slaves to obey *en haplotēti kardias phoboumenoi ton kyrion* — 'in singleness of heart, fearing the Lord' — collapsing the master-relationship into the God-relationship. Ephesians 6:5 says obey 'as you would Christ.' The household codes don't keep the categories clean. They explicitly route slave-obedience through the same vocabulary of fear and singleness of heart that Deuteronomy reserves for YHWH alone.

The critical reading (Balch, *Let Wives Be Submissive*; Horrell, *Solidarity and Difference*) is that the *Haustafeln* are first-century social-control documents that adapted the exclusive-loyalty language of Israelite monolatry to Greco-Roman household hierarchy because that was the only way the new Jesus-movement could survive in a slaveholding society. The contradiction is real — the household codes are doing something the Deuteronomic command was designed to prevent.

Verdict: the surface lexical distinction works for the simple case. The household codes' own language of *phobos* and *haplotēs kardias* dissolves it.

contradictions.question: Which came first: the calling of Peter and Andrew or the imprisonment of John the Baptist?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 4:12, 18-19 and Mark 1:14-17 both say Jesus began his Galilean ministry and called Peter and Andrew *after* John was imprisoned. John 1:35-42 has Andrew and Peter following Jesus while John is still actively baptizing — and John 3:22-24 makes the chronological framing explicit: *oupō gar ēn beblēmenos eis tēn phylakēn ho Iōannēs* — 'for John had not yet been thrown into prison.'
contradictions.commentary:
This is a Synoptic-vs-Johannine ordering problem and the Fourth Gospel knows exactly what it's doing.

Mark 1:14 sets the entire Galilean ministry timeline with one Greek phrase: *meta de to paradothēnai ton Iōannēn* — 'after John was handed over.' Matthew 4:12 carries this forward almost verbatim. In both Synoptics, the calling of Peter and Andrew at the lakeside (Mark 1:16-20; Matt 4:18-22) is the very first thing Jesus does after John's arrest. There's no ambiguity — the Synoptic narrative locks Peter's call into the post-arrest period.

John 1:35-42 tells a completely different story. Andrew is already a disciple of John the Baptist when he hears the Baptist identify Jesus as the Lamb of God. Andrew follows Jesus, finds his brother Simon, and brings him to Jesus, who renames him Cephas. This happens at the Jordan (John 1:28), not at the Sea of Galilee. John 3:22-24 then explicitly notes that John the Baptist was still baptizing and not yet imprisoned. The Fourth Gospel's author appears to be deliberately correcting or contradicting the Synoptic chronology.

The apologist harmonization — D. A. Carson in the Pillar volume, Andreas Köstenberger in the BECNT, Craig Blomberg in *The Historical Reliability of John's Gospel* — runs the two-stage call: John 1 is an initial meeting and tentative discipleship at the Jordan, and Mark/Matthew narrate a later, more formal call by the Sea of Galilee. The disciples went home to fishing in the interim, then Jesus 'called them again.' That's not impossible. The narrative grammar of Mark 1:16-17 doesn't explicitly say it's first contact.

But the Mark/Matthew passages read as initial-call narratives. The disciples drop everything immediately (*euthys aphentes ta diktya ēkolouthēsan autō* — 'immediately leaving the nets, they followed him,' Mark 1:18). There's no narrative signal of prior acquaintance. And John's *oupō ēn beblēmenos* in 3:24 is a deliberate parenthetical correction — the author is telling the reader 'the events I'm describing happened before John's imprisonment,' which is information that only matters if the audience is comparing to a different timeline (i.e., the Synoptic one).

The critical consensus (Brown, *AB John* 29; Schnackenburg; Bultmann) is that John 1-3 represents an independent tradition about Jesus's pre-Galilean ministry that is incompatible with the Synoptic compression of all activity into a post-arrest Galilean period. Matthew and Mark eliminate the Jordan ministry entirely; John insists on it. Both can't be giving us straight chronology.

Verdict: Mark/Matt put the call after John's arrest. John explicitly puts it before. The two-stage harmonization requires reading information into the Synoptic accounts that isn't there.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus heal Peter's mother in law before or after calling Peter?
contradictions.summary: Luke 4:38-39 has Jesus heal Peter's mother-in-law before Peter is called to discipleship in Luke 5:10-11. Matthew 4:18-19 reverses this — Peter is called at the lakeside first, and only later (Matthew 8:14-15) does Jesus heal his mother-in-law. The two evangelists put the same two events in opposite order.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of those ordering contradictions where the apologist concedes the Synoptics aren't trying to produce a strict chronology — and then has to live with the consequences of that concession.

Luke 4:38-39 has Jesus go from the Capernaum synagogue *into the house of Simon* (a Simon who hasn't been called yet in Luke's narrative) and heal his mother-in-law. Then in Luke 5:1-11 we get the miraculous catch of fish and Peter's call. The healing precedes the call by a full chapter.

Matthew 4:18-22 calls Peter at the lakeside as the inaugural act of the Galilean ministry. The Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5-7) intervenes. Then Matthew 8:14-15 has Jesus *enter Peter's house* and heal the mother-in-law. Call first, healing later.

Mark 1:16-31 splits the difference: Peter is called (1:16-18), and almost immediately afterward — same Sabbath day — Jesus heals the mother-in-law (1:29-31). Mark agrees with Matthew on order but not with the larger temporal gap.

The apologist harmonization, run by R. T. France in the NICNT Matthew and Darrell Bock in the BECNT Luke, is that Luke is using topical rather than chronological arrangement. Luke groups the Capernaum miracles (4:31-44) together for thematic reasons before backing up to narrate Peter's call in 5:1-11. This is the standard 'Synoptic ordering is theological, not chronological' move.

That works as a defense of Luke's literary craft but it's not a defense of the historical accuracy of the ordering. Luke's *eisēlthen eis tēn oikian Simōnos* — 'he entered the house of Simon' — in 4:38 reads as a passing reference to a Simon the audience is supposed to recognize. The problem is that Luke hasn't introduced Simon yet. Luke 5:1-11 narrates the call as if Peter is meeting Jesus for the first time (*exelthe ap' emou, hoti anēr hamartōlos eimi, kyrie* — 'depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord').

The critical consensus (Fitzmyer, *AB Luke* 28; Bovon *Hermeneia*; Marshall NIGTC) is that Luke knew Mark's ordering and deliberately rearranged it — pulling the Capernaum healings forward to anchor the ministry in a Galilean setting before backing up to a more dramatic call narrative. Matthew separately rearranged Mark's tight Sabbath cluster, pushing the mother-in-law healing forward by several chapters. The 'historical' ordering — if there was one — is unrecoverable.

Verdict: Luke and Matthew/Mark give the events in opposite order. The harmonization defends Luke's literary right to rearrange material but doesn't deliver a unified history.

contradictions.question: How did Peter and Andrew become Jesus's disciples?
contradictions.summary: Mark 1:16-17 and Matthew 4:18-19 have Jesus call Peter and Andrew while they are casting nets at the Sea of Galilee. John 1:35-42 has Andrew already a disciple of John the Baptist who, after hearing John identify Jesus as the Lamb of God, follows Jesus on his own and then brings Peter. Luke 5:4-11 has yet a third version — Peter is called after a miraculous catch of fish that nearly sinks the boats. Three irreconcilable call narratives for the same disciples.
contradictions.commentary:
Three gospels, three different mechanisms for how the same two men became disciples. This is the classic Synoptic-plus-John call problem.

Mark/Matthew version: Jesus walks past, sees brothers fishing, says 'Follow me,' they drop the nets and follow. No prior acquaintance, no fish miracle, no John the Baptist context.

John version: Andrew is already a disciple of John the Baptist. John points to Jesus and calls him *ho amnos tou theou* — the Lamb of God. Andrew and another disciple (probably the Beloved Disciple) spend the day with Jesus. Andrew then finds Peter and brings him — Peter doesn't get called by Jesus directly; he's recruited by his brother. The setting is the Jordan, not Galilee.

Luke version: Jesus borrows Peter's boat to preach from, then tells Peter to put out into the deep. Peter (already addressing Jesus as *epistata*, master) protests but obeys. The catch is so massive the nets break. Peter falls at Jesus's knees and Jesus says *mē phobou, apo tou nyn anthrōpous esē zōgrōn* — 'don't fear, from now on you will be catching men.' The boats are brought ashore and Peter, James, and John leave everything to follow. No reference to John the Baptist, no separate Andrew tradition.

The apologist harmonization runs in two layers. Layer one — Carson, Köstenberger, Blomberg — sequences the events: John 1 = initial Jordan encounter; Luke 5 = the miraculous catch as a renewed/formal call at Galilee; Mark/Matt = same Galilee call, abbreviated. So three different gospels are giving you three different cross-sections of the same multi-stage call. Layer two — the typical apologetic move — emphasizes that the call wasn't a single event but a progressive deepening of commitment.

The problem is that the texts don't support this layering. Mark 1:18 says they followed *immediately* — no signal of a prior call. John 1:42 has Jesus rename Simon as Cephas at the Jordan — which Mark 3:16 and Matthew 16:18 both treat as later events, with very different settings. Luke 5:8 has Peter call himself *anēr hamartōlos* — 'a sinful man' — in a way that reads as an initial revelation of Jesus's identity, not a recommitment.

The critical reading (Brown *AB John*; Fitzmyer *AB Luke*; Marcus *AB Mark*; Davies-Allison ICC) is that we have three independent traditions about how Peter became a disciple. The earliest layer probably had Peter as a fisherman called at the lakeside (a tradition Q-adjacent, preserved in Mark). John's gospel deliberately recast this with a Baptist-tradition framing to undercut competing Baptist-sect Christology. Luke composed (or expanded) the miraculous-catch tradition to give Peter a dramatic conversion-moment matching his later prominence — note the parallel to John 21:1-14 where the miraculous catch reappears in a post-resurrection setting.

Verdict: there is no parsimonious way to read these as one event. The harmonization either invents a multi-stage process the texts don't narrate, or it forces three independent traditions into a single contrived chronology. Take your pick: Synoptics are right, John is right, or none of them are reporting straight history.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus preach his first sermon on a mountain or a plain?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 5:1 has Jesus go up *eis to oros* (into the mountain) and deliver the Sermon on the Mount. Luke 6:17 has him *come down with them and stand on a level place* (*epi topou pedinou*) before delivering the parallel Sermon on the Plain. Same general teaching block, same opening beatitudes, two different physical settings.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the classic Synoptic-parallel problems and the apologist defense actually has some force — but not enough to make the harmonization parsimonious.

Matthew 5:1 — *idōn de tous ochlous anebē eis to oros* — 'seeing the crowds he went up into the mountain.' Matthew 8:1, after the sermon ends, then says *katabantos de autou apo tou orous* — 'when he came down from the mountain.' The mountain framing brackets the entire Sermon on the Mount.

Luke 6:12 has Jesus go up *eis to oros* to pray and choose the Twelve. Then Luke 6:17 has him *katabas met' autōn* — 'coming down with them' — and standing *epi topou pedinou* — 'on a level/flat place.' The beatitudes and woes follow.

The apologist harmonization, run for centuries (Augustine in *De consensu evangelistarum*, Carson in EBC, France in NICNT), is that the *topos pedinos* of Luke 6:17 is a plateau on the mountainside — a level place on the mountain, not a separate plain at sea level. Jesus comes down from the higher prayer-summit to a flat shelf, and the larger crowd gathers there. Matthew is summarizing the same event from the elevated-mountain perspective.

The textual problem is that the two sermons aren't actually the same sermon. Matthew's Sermon on the Mount runs 107 verses of teaching material (Matt 5:3-7:27, bracketed by the setting in 5:1-2 and the response in 7:28-29). Luke's Sermon on the Plain runs 30 verses (Luke 6:20-49). They share core material — beatitudes, love of enemies, judging, the house on the rock — but Matthew's version is roughly three times longer and contains substantial material (the antitheses 'you have heard it said... but I say to you,' the Lord's Prayer, the foxes and birds saying) that Luke distributes elsewhere in his gospel (Luke 11, 12, 13).

The critical consensus (Davies-Allison ICC; Luz *Hermeneia*; Fitzmyer *AB Luke* 28A; Bovon *Hermeneia*) is that both Matthew and Luke are working from a shared Q source containing the core sermon material, and each evangelist has expanded and arranged it differently. Matthew has clustered Jesus's teaching into the five great discourses (chs 5-7, 10, 13, 18, 24-25) of which the Sermon on the Mount is the first; Luke has distributed the same material across his travel narrative. The mountain/plain difference is a literary-theological choice — Matthew is staging Jesus as a new Moses delivering law from a new Sinai; Luke is staging Jesus among the people on level ground.

The mountain-plateau harmonization is technically possible — *topos pedinos* can mean a level patch on elevated terrain. But it's a post-hoc reconciliation of what the texts present as two distinct settings. And it doesn't address the larger structural divergence: the sermons have different lengths, different content distribution, and different audiences (Matthew has just the disciples until 7:28; Luke has the disciples *and* a great multitude).

Verdict: the level-place-on-the-mountain harmonization buys the setting at the cost of conceding the sermons are differently composed. The two pericopes are best understood as redactional reworkings of Q material, not two reports of the same historical event.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus come to bring peace?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 5:9 blesses peacemakers; Luke 2:14 has the angels announce 'on earth peace'; John 14:27 and 16:33 have Jesus give peace to his disciples; Acts 10:36 says God sent the word to Israel 'preaching peace by Jesus Christ.' Then Matthew 10:34 has Jesus say *ouk ēlthon balein eirēnēn alla machairan* — 'I came not to bring peace but a sword' — and Luke 12:51 explicitly denies that he came to give peace, promising household division instead.
contradictions.commentary:
The apologist response here is partially correct on the lexicography, and the contradiction can be softened in places — but Matthew 10:34 is doing exactly what the SAB says it's doing.

The 'peace' passages span a range of semantic fields. Luke 2:14's *eirēnē* is liturgical-angelic announcement language echoing Isaianic shalom oracles. John 14:27's *eirēnēn aphiēmi hymin, eirēnēn tēn emēn didōmi hymin* is internal/spiritual peace explicitly contrasted with the kind 'the world gives.' Acts 10:36 is missionary-summary vocabulary. Matthew 5:9 commands peacemaking as discipleship ethic.

The apologist harmonization, run by Blomberg in his Matthew NAC and by Carson in EBC, distinguishes between (1) eschatological/spiritual peace that Jesus brings between God and humanity, and (2) social-political peace that Jesus disrupts because allegiance to him divides households. Two senses of *eirēnē*, no contradiction. That's a defensible reading of John 14:27 in particular, where Jesus *explicitly* contrasts his peace with worldly peace.

But Matthew 10:34 doesn't fit that frame. Jesus says *mē nomisēte hoti ēlthon balein eirēnēn epi tēn gēn* — 'do not think I came to bring peace on the earth.' *Epi tēn gēn* — 'on the earth' — is the same phrase the angels use in Luke 2:14 (*epi gēs eirēnē*). Jesus is denying exactly what the angels announce. And he says he came to bring *machairan* — a sword. Luke 12:51 doubles down: *dokeite hoti eirēnēn paregenomēn dounai en tē gē? ouchi, legō hymin, all' ē diamerismon* — 'do you think I came to give peace on the earth? No, I tell you, but rather division.'

The critical reading (Allison, *The End of the Ages Has Come*; Davies-Allison ICC; Luz *Hermeneia*) is that Matthew 10:34 and Luke 12:51 preserve a genuinely sharp-edged eschatological saying — likely from Q — about the apocalyptic urgency of the kingdom dividing families. This sits alongside other equally apocalyptic Jesus material (the Q passages on hating father and mother, leaving the dead to bury their dead, the broken-up household). The 'peace' sayings in John and Luke 2 reflect later theological development as the apocalyptic edge softened into a more spiritualized message of internal peace.

The two-senses-of-peace harmonization works for John 14 and Acts 10. It does not work for the direct angel-vs-Jesus contradiction between Luke 2:14 and Matthew 10:34. The angels' announcement and Jesus's self-description are in the same gospel-canon using the same Greek phrase and giving opposite content.

Verdict: Jesus came to bring peace (some places). Jesus explicitly denies coming to bring peace (other places). The two-senses move smooths some friction but not the central angel-vs-Jesus collision.

contradictions.question: Should we let others see our good works?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 5:16 commands disciples to let their light shine before others *hopōs idōsin hymōn ta kala erga* — 'so that they may see your good works' — and 1 Peter 2:12 echoes this in nearly identical language. Just one chapter later, Matthew 6:1 warns *prosechete tēn dikaiosynēn hymōn mē poiein emprosthen tōn anthrōpōn pros to theathēnai autois* — 'beware of practicing your righteousness before others to be seen by them.' Same gospel, two consecutive chapters, opposite instruction.
contradictions.commentary:
This is an in-house Matthew contradiction and the apologist response actually has the cleanest possible distinction available — the question is whether that distinction holds up under scrutiny.

Matthew 5:16 uses *kala erga* (good works) and the *hopōs* (purpose) clause says explicitly *hopōs ... doxasōsin ton patera hymōn* — 'so that they may glorify your Father.' The visibility is instrumentalized toward God's glory.

Matthew 6:1 uses *dikaiosynē* (righteousness, especially almsgiving — verses 2-4 narrow it to *eleēmosynē*) and the purpose clause is *pros to theathēnai autois* — 'in order to be seen by them.' Reward language follows: practice your righteousness publicly and you forfeit your reward from the Father.

The apologist distinction — Carson EBC, Blomberg NAC, France NICNT, Hagner WBC — is motivational, not visibility-based. Both passages permit visible good works; the difference is whether the visibility is the *goal* (6:1, forbidden) or a *byproduct* of authentic piety (5:16, commanded). Same external behavior, opposite internal motive.

That distinction is lexically defensible. The Greek does support it. 5:16's *doxasōsin ton patera hymōn* makes the audience's God-glorification the telos; 6:1's *pros to theathēnai autois* makes their human-praise the telos.

But here's where the apologist reading runs into 6:3 — *mē gnōtō hē aristera sou ti poiei hē dexia sou* — 'do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.' The instruction is not 'do alms publicly but for the right reason' — it's 'do alms so secretly that even you don't track them.' And 6:6 on prayer: *eiselthe eis to tameion sou kai kleisas tēn thyran sou proseuxai tō patri sou tō en tō kryptō* — 'go into your inner room and shut the door and pray to your Father in secret.' The recommended behavior is *invisible*, not merely 'visible but well-motivated.'

The critical reading (Davies-Allison ICC; Luz *Hermeneia*; Betz on the Sermon) is that 5:16 and 6:1-18 reflect two distinct teaching traditions that the Matthean redactor stitched together without fully reconciling. 5:16 likely derives from a Jewish-Christian missiological context where Gentile observers seeing exemplary lives was instrumental to evangelization. 6:1-18 derives from a Jewish piety tradition (probably independent of the lamp-saying) that prizes hidden righteousness as the only kind that earns divine reward. The motivational-distinction harmonization papers over this by emphasizing 5:16 and de-emphasizing 6:3-6's actual instruction to hide one's piety.

Verdict: the motivational distinction works for 5:16 vs 6:1 narrowly construed. It does not work for 5:16 vs 6:3-6 ('hide it from yourself'). Matthew preserves two traditions whose practical instructions point in opposite directions.

contradictions.question: Is it OK to add to the law of Moses?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 4:2 forbids adding to the commandments: *lōʾ tōsipû ʿal-haddābār ʾăšer ʾānōkî mĕṣawweh ʾetkem* — 'you shall not add to the word which I command you.' Matthew 5:21-22 has Jesus extend the Decalogue's prohibition of murder to cover anger and insult — explicitly adding new content to Mosaic law with the formula *ēkousate hoti errethē ... egō de legō hymin* — 'you have heard that it was said ... but I say to you.'
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleaner examples of the New Testament's covenant-expansion problem running headlong into the Torah's no-addition clause.

Deuteronomy 4:2 in Hebrew is unambiguous: *lōʾ tōsipû ʿal-haddābār* — 'do not add to the word.' The verse pairs the prohibition with *wĕlōʾ tigrĕʿû mimmennû* — 'and do not subtract from it.' Deuteronomy 12:32 (Heb 13:1) repeats the same formula. The Torah's self-protective canon-clause is explicit: the Mosaic law as given is complete and not to be supplemented.

Matthew 5:21-22 has Jesus quote the Sixth Commandment (*ou phoneuseis* — 'you shall not murder') and then expand it: anyone angry with his brother is liable to judgment, anyone who says *rhaka* is liable to the council, anyone who says *mōre* (fool) is liable to the fire of Gehenna. The Greek formula *ēkousate hoti errethē tois archaiois ... egō de legō hymin* is structurally a contrastive expansion. Whether Jesus is intensifying the commandment or replacing it is a long-debated question among critical scholars, but either way, he's adding content the Mosaic text doesn't contain.

The standard apologist harmonization — Carson EBC, Blomberg NAC, France NICNT, Wright NTPG — distinguishes between (1) adding to Torah and (2) interpreting/intensifying Torah. Jesus isn't adding new commands; he's revealing the deeper intent of existing commands. Anger is the root from which murder grows; addressing the root is exegesis, not addition.

That works as theology and it works for some of the antitheses (the murder-anger one, arguably). It works less well for the divorce antithesis (5:31-32), where Jesus narrows what Deuteronomy 24:1-4 explicitly permits — that's *subtraction* from Torah, also forbidden by Deut 4:2. And it works less well for the swearing antithesis (5:33-37), where Jesus's *mē omosai holōs* — 'do not swear at all' — overrides Numbers 30 and Deuteronomy 23:21-23 which legislate oath-keeping. The 'interpretation not addition' defense becomes harder to sustain across the full antithesis block.

The critical reading (Davies-Allison ICC; Luz *Hermeneia*; Allison, *The New Moses*) is that Matthew is staging Jesus as a new Moses delivering an expanded/revised Torah from a new Sinai (the mountain in 5:1). Matthew's Christology requires Jesus to have authority *over* the Mosaic law, which is precisely the authority Deuteronomy 4:2 reserves to no human. The antitheses are best understood as Matthew's claim that Jesus stands in the position God occupies in Deut 4:2 — the one whose words may not be added to or subtracted from. Whether you call that 'addition' or 'replacement,' it's a violation of Deuteronomy 4:2's plain meaning.

Verdict: Deut 4:2 forbids addition; Matthew 5 visibly adds content. The 'just interpretation' defense smooths some antitheses but breaks on the divorce and oath antitheses where Jesus narrows or overrides explicit Torah legislation.

contradictions.question: Is divorce ever permissible?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 24:1-2 permits divorce for any 'uncleanness' (Hebrew *ʿerwat dābār*) — historically read liberally by the school of Hillel as covering almost any cause. Matthew 5:32 and 19:9 restrict divorce to cases of *porneia* (fornication/sexual immorality). 1 Corinthians 7:15 adds a Pauline exception for desertion by an unbelieving spouse. Mark 10:11 and Luke 16:18 prohibit divorce-and-remarriage absolutely, without any exception clause. Four different positions across the canon.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the most-studied internal divergences in the New Testament because it's not just a Torah-vs-Jesus problem — it's a Jesus-vs-Jesus problem, since the same evangelist (Matthew) has the exception clause while Mark and Luke don't.

Deuteronomy 24:1 — *kî yimṣāʾ-bāh ʿerwat dābār* — 'because he has found some unseemly thing in her.' The phrase *ʿerwat dābār* is famously ambiguous. The Mishnah (*m. Gittin* 9:10) records the dispute: Shammai restricted it to sexual immorality; Hillel permitted divorce 'even if she spoiled his dish'; Akiba permitted it 'even if he found another more beautiful.' Second Temple Judaism had wide-open legal divorce.

Mark 10:11-12 — *hos an apolysē tēn gynaika autou kai gamēsē allēn moichatai ep' autēn* — 'whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her.' No exception clause. Luke 16:18 is identical in substance. This is the earliest layer of the Jesus tradition on divorce.

Matthew 5:32 and 19:9 add *parektos logou porneias* (5:32) and *mē epi porneia* (19:9) — 'except for *porneia*.' Most critical scholars (Davies-Allison, Luz, Hagner) see these as Matthean redactional additions to soften the absolute Markan prohibition for a Matthean community that needed a halakhic exception clause. The Greek *porneia* itself is contested — it could mean adultery (the Shammaite reading), incestuous marriage within forbidden degrees (the Fitzmyer reading, paralleled by CD 4:20-5:2 at Qumran), or fornication more broadly.

1 Corinthians 7:15 — Paul adds his own exception (*ei de ho apistos chōrizetai, chōrizesthō* — 'but if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so'). Paul explicitly distinguishes this from Jesus's teaching ('not I but the Lord' in 7:10, then 'I, not the Lord' in 7:12). Paul knows he's extending the original prohibition.

The apologist harmonization — Heth and Wenham *Jesus and Divorce*, John Murray *Divorce*, Instone-Brewer *Divorce and Remarriage in the Bible* — runs several lines. Most commonly: Mark and Luke abbreviate; Matthew preserves the original Shammaite-influenced exception; Paul applies the principle to a new pastoral situation; all are consistent under a comprehensive Christian-marriage ethic. Some defenders (especially Catholic interpreters) read Matthew's *porneia* very narrowly as illicit-degree-of-kinship marriages so that no 'real' marriage can ever be ended.

The critical reading is that we're watching a tradition develop in front of us. Mark's absolute prohibition (likely closer to the historical Jesus, per Crossan, Sanders, Meier *Marginal Jew* vol 4) is too rigorous for first-century communities to live with. Matthew softens it. Paul extends the softening. Deuteronomy is the Torah baseline that the Jesus tradition is consciously tightening. The four-position canon reflects four different communities at different stages negotiating real marriages against an evolving teaching.

Verdict: the four positions do not collapse into one without significant redactional argument. The harmonization that says 'Mark abbreviates, Matthew completes' requires postulating that Mark and Luke independently dropped a clause both their respective communities would have desperately wanted to keep.

contradictions.question: Is anyone good?
contradictions.summary: Isaiah 64:6 says all human righteousness is *kĕbeged ʿiddîm* — 'as filthy rags' — and the Pauline literature builds an entire doctrine of universal depravity on this and similar verses. Luke 23:50 then describes Joseph of Arimathea as *anēr agathos kai dikaios* — 'a good and just man.' The same canon that insists no one is good has narrators describing specific individuals as good.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a question about whether the Bible's universal-depravity passages and its particular-virtue descriptions can be held in the same hand. The apologist response actually works pretty well for most of the canon — Luke 23:50 is the awkward outlier.

Isaiah 64:6 (MT 64:5) in context is a communal lament about exilic Israel's collective failure — *wattĕmaʿăṭēnû bĕyad-ʿăwōnēnû* — 'and you have melted us in the hand of our iniquity.' The 'filthy rags' line is a corporate confession in a specific historical moment, not a metaphysical statement about every individual being incapable of any virtue. Reading it as universal anthropological pessimism (the Augustinian/Calvinist move) requires lifting it out of its lament-genre context.

Paul does something similar in Romans 3:10-12, quoting Psalm 14:1-3 ('there is none who does good, no not one'). The Psalm in its original Hebrew context is about *bĕnê ʾādām* who have gone astray, not a metaphysical claim that no human being can ever be virtuous. Romans 3 weaponizes it for theological purposes.

Meanwhile the Hebrew Bible repeatedly describes specific people as *ṣaddîq* (righteous): Noah was *ʾîš ṣaddîq tāmîm hāyāh bĕdōrōtāyw* — 'a righteous man, blameless in his generations' (Gen 6:9). Job is described by God himself as *ʾîš tām wĕyāšār* — 'blameless and upright' (Job 1:8). Luke 1:6 calls Zechariah and Elizabeth *dikaioi amphoteroi enantion tou theou* — 'both righteous before God.' And Luke 23:50 calls Joseph of Arimathea *anēr agathos kai dikaios*.

More directly relevant: Jesus in Mark 10:18 (and Luke 18:19) responds to being called 'good teacher' with *ti me legeis agathon? oudeis agathos ei mē heis ho theos* — 'why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.' That's a clean denial that anyone but God is *agathos*. Luke himself then turns around in 23:50 and uses *agathos* of Joseph of Arimathea. Luke contradicts Luke's own Jesus.

The apologist harmonization — Carson, Bock BECNT Luke, the IVP *Hard Sayings* commentary — distinguishes between (1) relative goodness (humans compared to other humans) and (2) absolute goodness (only God). On that reading Joseph of Arimathea is relatively good while still being unable to claim absolute goodness in God's sight. Same word, two senses.

The distinction is real in theology but the Greek text doesn't mark it. *Agathos* is *agathos*. When Luke applies it to Joseph and Jesus denies it of everyone but God, the same lexical item is doing both jobs. The contradiction is in the canon's flat-footed use of the same word.

Verdict: the lament-genre context softens Isaiah 64:6 significantly. The harder problem is Jesus's *oudeis agathos* in Mark 10:18/Luke 18:19 vs. Luke 23:50's *anēr agathos*. The relative-vs-absolute defense works as theology but doesn't track the Greek vocabulary the texts actually use.

contradictions.question: Should Christians pray in public?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 6:5-6 explicitly forbids public prayer: do not be like the hypocrites who pray in synagogues and street corners to be seen — go into your inner room (*tameion*) and shut the door. John 11:41-42 has Jesus pray publicly at the tomb of Lazarus and explicitly say he did so 'because of the crowd standing around.' 1 Timothy 2:8 commands men to pray 'in every place' (*en panti topō*) lifting holy hands.
contradictions.commentary:
This is another in-house Matthew problem extended across the canon, and the apologist motivational-distinction is the same as for entry 407 — with the same limits.

Matthew 6:5-6 is the strict text: *otan proseuchēsthe ouk esesthe hōs hoi hypokritai, hoti philousin en tais synagōgais kai en tais gōniais tōn plateiōn hestōtes proseuchesthai, hopōs phanōsin tois anthrōpois* — 'when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, for they love to pray standing in synagogues and on street corners so as to be seen by people.' The recommended alternative is the *tameion* — the storeroom or inner chamber, the most private space in a Palestinian house. The instruction is concrete: pray in private, with the door closed.

John 11:41-42 has Jesus pray standing at Lazarus's tomb, in front of a crowd, and explicitly say *dia ton ochlon ton periestōta eipon, hina pisteusōsin* — 'because of the crowd standing around I said it, so that they might believe.' That's exactly the *pros to theathēnai* (to be seen) motivation Matthew 6:5 condemns — except John frames it as legitimate because the visibility serves an evangelistic purpose.

1 Timothy 2:8 — *boulomai oun proseuchesthai tous andras en panti topō* — 'I will therefore that men pray in every place' — recommends public prayer across multiple settings.

Acts is loaded with public prayer scenes: the assembled disciples in the upper room (Acts 1:14, 24), the apostles at Pentecost, Peter and John praying in the temple (Acts 3:1), Stephen's prayer at his execution, the prayers at Paul's farewells (Acts 20:36, 21:5). The New Testament practice of the early church is publicly assembled prayer.

The apologist motivational-distinction harmonization — Carson EBC, France NICNT, Mounce on the Pastorals — distinguishes between (1) ostentatious prayer aimed at human admiration (forbidden) and (2) corporate/communal prayer or prayer in genuine public service (permitted). The Matthew 6 prohibition is about the heart, not the venue.

That's reasonable as theology and probably captures what Matthew's redactor was trying to do. But Matthew 6:5-6 doesn't actually mark the distinction the way the apologist needs it to. The instruction isn't 'don't pray for showy reasons' — it's 'pray in the *tameion* with the door shut.' The recommended behavior is invisibility. If Matthew wanted to permit corporate prayer with the right motive, he could have said so, and he didn't.

The critical reading (Davies-Allison ICC; Luz *Hermeneia*; Betz on the Sermon) is that Matthew 6:5-6 is part of a hidden-piety teaching block (6:1-18) that derives from a Jewish-piety tradition emphasizing covert almsgiving, prayer, and fasting. It sits uncomfortably alongside Matthew's own Lord's Prayer (6:9-13) which presumes communal usage, and against the broader New Testament's normalization of corporate prayer. The redactor inherited the hidden-piety material and didn't fully harmonize it with the rest of his community's practice.

Verdict: the motivational defense smooths the question for most NT public prayers. It struggles to deliver Matthew 6:6's *eiselthe eis to tameion sou kai kleisas tēn thyran sou* — 'go into your inner room and shut the door' — as anything other than a directive to private rather than public prayer.

contradictions.question: Do Christians know how to pray?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 6:9-13 has Jesus teach the Lord's Prayer with the formula *houtōs oun proseuchesthe hymeis* — 'therefore pray in this way.' Romans 8:26 then says *to gar ti proseuxōmetha katho dei ouk oidamen* — 'for we do not know what to pray for as we ought' — and only the Spirit's wordless intercession makes Christian prayer possible. So the question is whether Jesus actually equipped his disciples to pray.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a weaker contradiction than most in the batch — the apologist response can carry a lot of weight here, though there's still a thin tension worth flagging.

Matthew 6:9-13 (and its Lukan parallel 11:2-4) is Jesus giving a model prayer in answer to the disciples' request *kyrie, didaxon hēmas proseuchesthai* — 'Lord, teach us to pray' (Luke 11:1). The Lord's Prayer is a *template* — petitions for God's name to be hallowed, kingdom to come, daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from testing. It teaches *what* to pray for and *how* to structure the petition.

Romans 8:26 is doing something different. Paul writes *hōsautōs de kai to pneuma synantilambanetai tē astheneia hēmōn* — 'likewise the Spirit also helps our weakness' — *to gar ti proseuxōmetha katho dei ouk oidamen* — 'for we do not know what to pray for as we ought.' The context is suffering, eschatological groaning, and the inadequacy of human articulation in the face of cosmic distress. The Spirit intercedes *stenagmois alalētois* — 'with inarticulate groanings.'

The apologist harmonization — Cranfield ICC, Moo NICNT, Schreiner BECNT — is that the two passages address different aspects of prayer. The Lord's Prayer provides the form and content; Romans 8:26 addresses the existential depth of prayer in suffering, where even with a model in hand, the believer doesn't know what to ask for. The Spirit's intercession is not a substitute for the disciple's prayer but a help to it.

That reading is defensible and probably what Paul is actually saying. *Katho dei* — 'as we ought' — qualifies the lack of knowledge. The believer can pray; what's lacking is the deep wisdom about *what to pray for in any given trouble*. The Lord's Prayer teaches the basic shape; the Spirit fills in the specifics no creature can know.

The thin tension that survives is this: Romans 8:26 says *ouk oidamen* — 'we do not know' — without qualifying it to 'we don't know in deep suffering.' Paul's broader frame in Romans 8 is the universal human condition under the *douleia tēs phthoras* (slavery to corruption, 8:21), not a specific subset of trying-hard cases. If the Lord's Prayer fully equipped Christians to pray, the unqualified *ouk oidamen* is awkward. Paul is functioning as if the Lord's Prayer doesn't fully solve the problem.

The critical reading (Jewett *Hermeneia* Romans; Käsemann *Romans*) is that Paul's pneumatology in Romans 8 is operating in a different register than the Synoptic catechesis. Paul wrote before the Synoptics were composed and doesn't show direct knowledge of the Lord's Prayer tradition. The two passages reflect different theological streams of early Christian prayer-practice — a Jewish-Christian catechetical stream (Matthew/Luke) and a Pauline pneumatological stream — that the eventual canon places side by side without harmonizing.

Verdict: the apologist 'different aspects of prayer' defense works fairly well. The thin tension is that Paul's *ouk oidamen* is unqualified in a way that doesn't quite line up with 'we have a model from Jesus.' Not a slam-dunk contradiction, but not nothing either.

contradictions.question: Is God's will always done in heaven?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 6:10 has Jesus teach disciples to pray *genēthētō to thelēma sou, hōs en ouranō kai epi gēs* — 'your will be done, as in heaven so on earth' — taking the perfect obedience of heaven as the model for which earth is the petition. Revelation 12:7 then has *egeneto polemos en tō ouranō* — 'there was war in heaven' — between Michael and the dragon. War in heaven is a strange backdrop for a kingdom in which God's will is always done.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a weaker contradiction than it looks at first, but it does open onto a real cosmological tension in the canon.

Matthew 6:10's petition assumes heaven is the locus of God's perfectly executed will. The clause *hōs en ouranō kai epi gēs* takes heaven's obedience as the standard and asks for that standard to extend to earth. The grammar presupposes that heaven currently exemplifies what earth currently lacks.

Revelation 12:7-9 — *egeneto polemos en tō ouranō, ho Michaēl kai hoi angeloi autou tou polemēsai meta tou drakontos* — 'there was war in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon.' The dragon and his angels are defeated and cast down to earth. This war presupposes a heavenly realm in which (a) a powerful evil being can operate, and (b) battle is required to remove him. That doesn't sit easily with a heaven in which God's will is already perfectly enacted.

The apologist harmonization — Beale NIGTC Revelation, Mounce NICNT, Aune WBC — runs two paths. Path one: the war in Revelation 12 is a *past* heavenly event (the primordial fall of Satan), already concluded, so heaven's current state is one of restored perfect obedience. Path two: heaven in apocalyptic literature is a complex multi-tiered space (cf. 2 Cor 12:2's *tritou ouranou* — third heaven), and war happens in lower heavens while God's will reigns absolutely in the highest. Both moves have textual support.

But Revelation 12:7's *egeneto* is an aorist that the wider Christian tradition has read as eschatologically present — the war between Michael and the dragon mapping the church's experience under persecution (cf. Rev 12:11). The dragon's expulsion is what makes the persecution intensify on earth (12:12). The apocalypse is staging cosmic conflict that resists being tidily relegated to either a primordial past or a separate sub-heaven.

The broader canonical issue is that the Hebrew Bible itself doesn't present heaven as a place of monolithic obedience. The *bĕnê hāʾĕlōhîm* assemble in 1 Kings 22:19-22 and disagree among themselves about how to entice Ahab. Job 1-2 has Satan walking into the divine council and arguing with God. The *Bĕnê hāʾĕlōhîm* in Genesis 6:1-4 rebelliously take human wives. Daniel 10 has the prince of Persia delaying Gabriel for 21 days. Heaven in pre-Christian Jewish cosmology is *not* a place where God's will is automatically and immediately enacted — it's a court populated by other beings who push back.

The critical reading (Collins *Apocalyptic Imagination*; Mark Smith *Origins of Biblical Monotheism*; Aune WBC Revelation) is that Matthew 6:10's monolithically obedient heaven represents a later Christianized cosmology that doesn't fully cohere with the older Hebrew Bible and Second Temple Jewish conception that Revelation 12 preserves. The two represent different cosmological strata in the canon.

Verdict: the past-event harmonization works narrowly. The broader Hebrew Bible/Second Temple cosmology of heaven-as-contested-divine-council sits uneasily with the Lord's Prayer's heaven-as-perfect-obedience. The contradiction is thin at the specific verse level but deeper in the canon-wide cosmology.

contradictions.question: Should Christians be concerned with material things?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 6:31, 34 has Jesus instruct disciples to take no thought (*mē merimnēsēte*) for food, drink, clothing, or the morrow. 1 Timothy 5:8 then says if anyone *tōn idiōn kai malista oikeiōn ou pronoei, tēn pistin ērnētai* — 'does not provide for his own, especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.' One text forbids material anxiety; the other makes material provision a test of authentic faith.
contradictions.commentary:
This contradiction turns on the semantic range of the Greek words involved, and the apologist response does meaningful lexical work — but the underlying tension between Synoptic ethics and Pastoral ethics is real and well-documented in critical scholarship.

Matthew 6:25-34 uses *merimnaō* — to be anxious, to worry. The instruction is *mē merimnāte tē psychē hymōn* — 'do not be anxious for your life' — about what you'll eat, drink, wear. The reasoning is providential: the birds don't sow and the lilies don't spin, and the Father provides for them. Disciples are to seek first the kingdom and let tomorrow worry about itself.

1 Timothy 5:8 uses a different word: *pronoeō* — to plan ahead, to provide for, to take forethought for. Specifically *idiōn kai malista oikeiōn* — 'one's own, especially household.' The instruction is positive provision-making for dependent family members.

The apologist harmonization — Mounce on the Pastorals, Marshall ICC on the Pastorals, France NICNT Matthew — distinguishes (1) *merimna*-style anxiety, which is paralyzing fear about basic survival, from (2) *pronoia*-style forethought, which is responsible planning for dependents. Same lexical field is not the same instruction. Jesus condemns anxious distrust of God's provision; the Pastor commands prudent household management. No contradiction at the Greek lexical level.

This is a credible distinction. The Greek words really are different, and the conceptual fields really are distinguishable. *Merimna* is the worry that consumes; *pronoia* is the planning that enables. Stoic ethics worked with similar distinctions.

But the apologist defense glosses over how *demanding* Matthew 6:31-34 actually is. *Mē merimnēsēte eis tēn aurion* — 'do not be anxious about tomorrow' — combined with the parable's logic (the birds don't sow and reap, you should be even more cared for) is hard to square with running a household budget, planning for children's needs, saving against illness. The instruction isn't 'don't worry obsessively while still planning prudently'; it's 'consider the lilies — they neither toil nor spin.' Taken at face value, this is a radical eschatological ethic that presupposes the imminent kingdom is about to break in and ordinary economic forethought is obsolete.

The critical reading (Allison *The End of the Ages Has Come*; Theissen *The First Followers of Jesus*; Crossan *The Historical Jesus*) is that Matthew 6 preserves a genuine pre-70 Jesus-tradition wandering-charismatic ethic. Jesus and his early followers were itinerant prophets who did not work, did not save, and did not provide for households because they expected the end imminently. The Pastoral Epistles (whether or not authentically Pauline; the critical consensus is post-Pauline pseudepigrapha) reflect a second- or third-generation settled-church ethic where households need to be maintained over decades and the eschatological clock has slowed.

The lexical distinction between *merimna* and *pronoia* papers over what is genuinely a development from charismatic itinerancy to institutional household-Christianity. Both traditions are preserved in the canon. They don't fully cohere.

Verdict: the lexical distinction softens the surface contradiction in a defensible way. The underlying tension — Jesus's wandering-prophet ethic vs. the Pastorals' settled-household ethic — is real and is one of the standard fault lines critical scholarship has identified across the New Testament.

contradictions.question: Is casting out devils a sign of a true Christian?
contradictions.summary: Mark 16:17 (the disputed Longer Ending) lists casting out demons as one of the signs *parakolouthēsei tois pisteusasin* — 'that will follow those who believe.' Mark 9:38 and Luke 9:49 have the disciples report a non-follower casting out demons in Jesus's name, which Jesus permits. Matthew 7:22-23 has Jesus say that many who cast out demons in his name will hear *oudepote egnōn hymas* — 'I never knew you.' So exorcism either marks believers, marks any name-user, or marks people Jesus rejects.
contradictions.commentary:
The Mark 16:17 citation needs an immediate textual flag, and after that, the contradiction is real but the question framing is rough.

Mark 16:9-20 — the Longer Ending containing the casting-out-demons reference — is absent from the oldest and best Greek manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, both 4th century) and from the Old Syriac, the Sinaitic Syriac, and key Old Latin witnesses. It's also stylistically and vocabulary-different from authentic Mark. The critical consensus (Metzger *Textual Commentary*; NA28 apparatus; Marcus *AB Mark*) is that 16:9-20 is a secondary 2nd-century addition. The NRSV, NIV, ESV, and even most evangelical translations bracket or footnote it. Building a contradiction on Mark 16:17 means building it on a passage that probably wasn't original to the Gospel of Mark.

That said, the three positions extracted from the texts cited *are* in tension, and the tension survives even without Mark 16:17.

Mark 9:38-40 / Luke 9:49-50 — the disciples report *eidomen tina en tō onomati sou ekballonta daimonia* — 'we saw someone casting out demons in your name' — and forbade him *hoti ouk ēkolouthei hēmin* — 'because he did not follow us.' Jesus replies *mē kōlyete* — 'do not forbid him' — and adds *hos gar ouk estin kath' hēmōn, hyper hēmōn estin* — 'whoever is not against us is for us.' Exorcism in Jesus's name is presented as legitimate even by non-disciples.

Matthew 7:22-23 (Sermon on the Mount, no Markan parallel) — *polloi erousin moi en ekeinē tē hēmera, kyrie kyrie, ou tō sō onomati eprophēteusamen, kai tō sō onomati daimonia exebalomen?* — 'many will say to me on that day, Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name and in your name cast out demons?' And Jesus's answer: *oudepote egnōn hymas; apochōreite ap' emou hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian* — 'I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness.'

The apologist harmonization — Carson EBC, France NICNT, Davies-Allison ICC, Hagner WBC — distinguishes (a) exorcism as a *charismatic gift* that even unbelievers can wield by invoking Jesus's powerful name (cf. the sons of Sceva, Acts 19:13-16), from (b) exorcism as a sign of genuine discipleship. The same external act, three different inner relationships to Jesus. Mark 9 = legitimate even by outsiders; Matthew 7 = insufficient by itself; Mark 16 (if authentic) = expected of true believers.

That works as theology and probably tracks what the texts are actually doing. The contradiction is less 'do exorcisms prove Christianity' than 'how do we read exorcism semiotically' — and the canon gives nuanced answers that don't simply contradict.

Verdict: Mark 16:17 is textually suspect and shouldn't be the lead citation. The remaining tension between Mark 9 and Matthew 7 is more nuance than contradiction — exorcism is a permissible activity by outsiders (Mark 9) but cannot by itself authenticate discipleship (Matt 7). The two positions are compatible. The SAB question framing makes this look sharper than it is.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus know everything?
contradictions.summary: John 16:30 and 21:17 affirm that Jesus knows all things (*panta oidas*), and Colossians 2:2-3 says all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ. Mark 5:30-31 and Luke 8:45 have Jesus ask *tis hēpsato mou tōn himatiōn?* — 'who touched my garments?' — apparently not knowing who in the crowd had touched him. Mark 13:32 has Jesus deny knowing the day or hour of his return. The canon both ascribes and denies omniscience to Jesus.
contradictions.commentary:
This is the omniscience problem and it cuts through some of the deepest Christological waters in the New Testament. The apologist harmonization runs on the doctrine of the *kenosis* — and like a lot of high-Christology fixes, it does technical work but only by importing later doctrinal categories the texts themselves don't develop.

The omniscience-affirming texts are largely Johannine and Pauline. John 16:30 has the disciples say *nyn oidamen hoti oidas panta* — 'now we know that you know all things' — but this is the disciples' confession, not a direct narrator-claim. John 21:17 has Peter say *kyrie, panta sy oidas* — 'Lord, you know all things' — in a context of testing Peter's love, not exhaustively defining Jesus's epistemic state. Colossians 2:2-3 says *en hō eisin pantes hoi thēsauroi tēs sophias kai gnōseōs apokryphoi* — 'in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden' — which is a hymnic christological claim, not a discrete propositional inventory.

The omniscience-denying texts are more direct narrator-claims:

Mark 5:30 — Jesus *epignous en heautō tēn ex autou dynamin exelthousan* — 'perceiving in himself that power had gone out of him' — turns and says *tis mou hēpsato tōn himatiōn?* The question is genuine; the disciples laugh at him for asking (5:31). The woman has to come forward and confess. If Jesus knew, the question was theatrical; the narrative doesn't read that way.

Mark 13:32 / Matt 24:36 is the harder one — *peri de tēs hēmeras ekeinēs ē tēs hōras oudeis oiden, oude hoi angeloi en ouranō oude ho huios, ei mē ho patēr* — 'concerning that day or hour no one knows, not the angels in heaven nor the Son, but only the Father.' Jesus explicitly excludes himself from a particular knowledge-claim.

Luke 2:52 says *kai Iēsous proekopten en tē sophia* — 'and Jesus increased in wisdom' — which presupposes a non-omniscient baseline that grew over time.

The apologist harmonization, formalized at Chalcedon and run by every orthodox-Christology commentator since (Pannenberg, Macleod, Bauckham, Wright), is the *two natures* doctrine. Jesus has divine knowledge as God and limited human knowledge as man; in the incarnation he 'emptied himself' (Phil 2:7's *heauton ekenōsen*) of the active use of divine attributes while retaining them in his divine nature. The ignorance-passages reflect his human nature; the omniscience-passages reflect his divine nature.

That works as orthodox theology if you accept the Chalcedonian framework. But the New Testament texts themselves don't develop a two-natures epistemology. The canon's writers seem unaware of the problem they're creating. Mark just narrates Jesus not knowing who touched him; the redactor doesn't add a parenthesis explaining 'this was a question Jesus asked in his human nature.' Mark 13:32 is the cleanest denial of omniscience and it's spoken by Jesus himself, in his own voice, without qualification.

The critical reading (Brown *AB John*; Marcus *AB Mark*; Dunn *Christology in the Making*) is that the New Testament's Christology is developmental and inconsistent. Mark's Jesus is more limited than John's; Pauline-deutero-Pauline Christology (Colossians, Ephesians, Philippians 2) ascends higher still. The omniscience-question is a snapshot of that developmental trajectory: Mark's Jesus genuinely doesn't know things; John's Jesus knows all things; and these are different gospels' different Christologies, not different sides of the same metaphysical coin.

Verdict: the two-natures harmonization works as theology if you grant Chalcedon. It doesn't reflect what the gospel writers themselves were doing. Mark 5:30 and Mark 13:32 are texts that present Jesus as not knowing things, and pre-Chalcedonian Christianity took these at face value (which is why Arians, Adoptionists, and others built whole theologies on the limited-knowledge passages).

contradictions.question: What will happen to Jews when they die?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 8:12 has Jesus say that *hoi huioi tēs basileias ekblēthēsontai eis to skotos to exōteron* — 'the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into the outer darkness' — a phrase the SAB and a long Christian interpretive tradition has read as referring to ethnic Jews. Matthew 1:21 says Jesus came to save *ton laon autou apo tōn hamartiōn autōn* — 'his people from their sins' — and Romans 11:26 famously declares *kai houtōs pas Israēl sōthēsetai* — 'and so all Israel will be saved.' The canon both threatens Israel with damnation and promises Israel salvation.
contradictions.commentary:
The question framing here is loaded but the underlying tension is genuine, and it's one of the most-fought-over interpretive issues in Christian theology of Israel.

First the framing problem. Matthew 8:11-12 is the saying about many coming from east and west to dine with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, while *hoi huioi tēs basileias* are cast out. The SAB gloss identifies 'the sons of the kingdom' as 'the Jews,' but Matthew's own use of this phrase elsewhere (13:38, where 'the sons of the kingdom' are the wheat in the parable of the weeds, contrasted with 'sons of the evil one' as the weeds) makes it about religious response, not ethnicity. In the Matt 8 context, the saying responds to a Roman centurion's faith — Jesus is contrasting Gentiles who believe with co-ethnic Israelites who refuse. The 'sons of the kingdom' rejected here are unfaithful Israelites, not all Jews as such. Davies-Allison's ICC analysis (vol 2, pp. 27-32) is careful here.

That said, the broader tension is real. Romans 9-11 is Paul wrestling with exactly this problem: if Jesus is the messiah and most of Israel has rejected him, has God's promise to Israel failed? Paul's answer is the famous *pas Israēl sōthēsetai* — 'all Israel will be saved' — in Rom 11:26. What 'all Israel' means is a contested question — Cranfield ICC reads it as ethnic Israel restored in the eschaton; some Reformed interpreters (Calvin, N. T. Wright) read it as 'the totality of the elect, Jew and Gentile'; Jewett *Hermeneia* sees an eschatological-future restoration of ethnic Israel. Most critical scholarship reads Paul as committed to a future salvific work specifically for ethnic Israel.

Matthew 1:21 is more local: *autos gar sōsei ton laon autou* — 'he will save his people' — refers to his own ethnic people in the immediate Matthean context, then expands implicitly in later passages to include Gentile inclusion via the Great Commission.

The apologist harmonization — Carson, Blomberg, Moo on Romans — reads everything compatibly: Jesus came primarily for the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 15:24), some Israelites responded with faith and were saved as the remnant, others rejected and faced judgment (Matt 8:12), and Paul anticipates a future broader salvation of Israel at the eschaton (Rom 11:26). The texts can be read as a single coherent narrative if you accept the distinction between individual present judgment and corporate future restoration.

The critical reading splits two ways. One (Sanders, Räisänen) sees Matthew and Paul preserving incompatible Jewish-Christian theologies of Israel. Matthew's gospel — written after 70 CE for a Jewish-Christian community in conflict with the synagogue — is harsh toward unbelieving Jews (the parable of the wicked tenants in 21:33-46, the cry 'his blood be on us and our children' in 27:25). Paul, writing earlier and from a different social location, holds out a future for ethnic Israel that Matthew's later anti-synagogue polemic effectively cancels.

The other reading (Wright, Bird, Räisänen later) is that the texts reflect different stages of the same tradition working out the Israel-problem and can be held together as a complex but coherent eschatology.

The SAB framing of this as a binary 'hell or salvation' contradiction is too crude. The actual tension is between Matthew's anti-unfaithful-Israelite polemic (which the original context limits to specific unbelievers, but which later Christian tradition has tragically extended to all Jews) and Paul's future-restoration eschatology. Both are present in the canon, and they pull in different directions even if they don't formally contradict.

Verdict: the SAB framing is too binary. Matt 8:12 isn't actually about 'all Jews go to hell' — it's about unfaithful Israelites in a specific theological-narrative context. Romans 11:26 is about future eschatological restoration. The genuine tension is between Matthew's post-70 anti-synagogue polemic and Paul's pre-70 future-Israel hope — a tension that has had murderous consequences in Christian history and that critical scholarship recognizes as a real fault line.

contradictions.question: Was Jesus homeless?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 8:20 and Luke 9:58 have Jesus say *hai alōpekes phōleous echousin kai ta peteina tou ouranou kataskēnōseis, ho de huios tou anthrōpou ouk echei pou tēn kephalēn klinē* — 'foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.' Mark 2:1 and 2:15 reference Jesus being *en oikō* (at home) in Capernaum and entertaining guests. So either Jesus had no home or he had a house in Capernaum.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a contradiction the apologist response can largely defuse on a careful reading of the Greek prepositions and Markan geography — but a thin residue remains.

The homeless saying is Q material, preserved in Matt 8:20 = Luke 9:58. *Ouk echei pou tēn kephalēn klinē* — 'has nowhere to lay his head.' In context, both gospels deploy it as a response to a would-be follower who's asked to join Jesus's itinerant ministry. The point is the cost of discipleship — Jesus and his band are wanderers without settled accommodation.

The Markan 'at home' references need care. Mark 2:1 in the Greek says *eisēlthōn palin eis Kapharnaoum di' hēmerōn ēkousthē hoti en oikō estin* — 'when he entered again into Capernaum after some days, it was heard that he was *en oikō*.' The phrase *en oikō* — literally 'in a house' or 'at home' — is ambiguous. Translators have rendered it variously as 'at home,' 'in the house,' or 'indoors.' The most natural reading in a Capernaum context is the house of Simon Peter (Mark 1:29), which functioned as Jesus's Galilean base of operations during his ministry. Archaeological work at Capernaum — the so-called 'House of Peter,' a 1st-century structure venerated as a domus-ecclesia by the early Byzantine period (cf. Tzaferis, *Excavations at Capernaum*; Strange and Shanks BAR articles) — supports this reading.

Mark 2:15 is parallel: *kai ginetai katakeisthai auton en tē oikia autou* — 'and it happened that he was reclining in his house.' But whose house is 'his' here? The Greek pronoun *autou* is ambiguous. It could refer to Levi (the previous antecedent — Jesus has just called Levi the tax collector) or to Jesus. The Synoptic parallel in Luke 5:29 says explicitly *epoiēsen dochēn megalēn Leuis autō en tē oikia autou* — 'Levi made a great feast for him in his (Levi's) own house.' So Mark 2:15's 'his house' almost certainly means Levi's house, not Jesus's. Modern translations are split: NRSV reads 'sitting at dinner in Levi's house'; NIV reads 'having dinner at Levi's house.'

The apologist harmonization — Carson, France NICNT Mark, Marcus AB Mark — distinguishes between (1) Jesus having no *property* of his own (the homeless saying, accurate) and (2) Jesus using Peter's house as a Capernaum base during ministry stops (the Markan references, accurate). The homeless-saying is about itinerant ministry without a settled domicile of one's own; the Markan references are about being-a-guest in associates' homes. No contradiction.

That reading is exegetically sound. The Markan *en oikō* doesn't actually claim Jesus owned a house in Capernaum — it just narrates his presence in someone's domestic space (almost certainly Peter's). And the Q homeless-saying is about an itinerant lifestyle, not about lacking access to hospitality.

Where a thin residue remains: Mark 2:1's *en oikō* without specifying *whose* house, combined with the formulation *ēkousthē hoti en oikō estin* (it was heard that he was at home), sounds in Greek idiom much like a regular base or residence. Mark's audience may have assumed Jesus had a recognized Capernaum residence — whether owned or quasi-permanently borrowed from Peter — that functioned as 'home base.' The homeless-saying is then literary hyperbole pitched against the discipleship-call context.

Verdict: the apologist defense works. Jesus had no property; Jesus had a regular Capernaum base in Peter's house; the two are compatible. The SAB contradiction here is mostly a translation artifact — the KJV's flat 'the house' obscures what the Greek prepositions actually permit.

contradictions.question: How many men were possessed with devils?
contradictions.summary: Mark 5:1-2 and Luke 8:26-27 both narrate the Gerasene demoniac as *anthrōpos en pneumati akathartō* — a single man with an unclean spirit. Matthew 8:28 has the parallel encounter and gives *dyo daimonizomenoi* — 'two demon-possessed men.' Same lakeside crossing, same demon-named-Legion, two vs. one possessed.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of Matthew's signature doubling moves and it's a well-documented redactional pattern that critical scholarship has tracked across his gospel.

Mark 5:1-20 narrates a single demoniac: *anthrōpos en pneumati akathartō* (5:2) — 'a man with an unclean spirit' — who has been chained, broken his chains, lives among the tombs, cuts himself with stones, and is possessed by a demonic horde named Legion. After the exorcism into the swine, this one man asks to follow Jesus but is sent home to proclaim what God has done. Luke 8:26-39 follows Mark with the single-man version, adding only that he had been possessed *chronō hikanō* (for a long time) and *ouk emenen en oikia* (did not stay in a house). One demoniac in both Mark and Luke.

Matthew 8:28-34 has the same narrative — same place (though Matthew has Gadarenes, Mark has Gerasenes), same demon-named-Legion (though Matthew abbreviates), same swine, same dramatic outcome — but the demoniac is doubled: *hypēntēsan autō dyo daimonizomenoi* — 'two demoniacs met him.'

This isn't an isolated case. Matthew doubles in two other Markan healings:

1. The blind men of Jericho: Mark 10:46-52 has one blind man (Bartimaeus). Matthew 20:29-34 has two blind men, both unnamed.
2. The donkey of the triumphal entry: Mark 11:1-7 has one colt. Matthew 21:1-7 has a donkey *and* a colt (cf. entry 383 in this database).

The apologist harmonization — Carson, Blomberg, France NICNT — runs additive: there really were two demoniacs at Gerasa, two blind men at Jericho, and a donkey-plus-colt at Jerusalem. Mark just chose to focus on the more prominent member of each pair. The presence of two doesn't deny the presence of one; Matthew is supplying detail Mark omitted. Carson is particularly direct: 'Mark and Luke focus on the more prominent of the two.'

That works as a logical proposition — two doesn't formally contradict one if the 'one' is interpreted as 'one of two.' But it requires postulating that Mark independently chose to omit the second demoniac in the most dramatic single-demoniac story in the gospels, that Luke independently made the same omission, and that they did so in three separate cases. The pattern is too consistent to be coincidence.

The critical reading (Davies-Allison ICC; Luz *Hermeneia*; Held in Bornkamm-Barth-Held *Tradition and Interpretation*; Allison *Matthew* in *New Testament Theology* series) is that Matthew has a redactional tendency to double figures — a Matthean stylistic-theological choice, possibly to satisfy the *two-witness rule* of Deut 19:15 in Matthean ecclesiology (cf. Matt 18:16, where Jesus invokes the two-witness rule). Held's classic 1960 study made this case definitively and it's been broadly accepted across the critical commentary tradition. Matthew's doubled demoniacs and doubled blind men are redactional, not preservations of historical detail Mark dropped.

There's also a textual-critical note worth flagging: the place-name varies across the manuscript tradition — Gerasenes (Mark), Gadarenes (Matt), Gergesenes (a Caesarea-Origen variant). Origen himself noted Gerasa is ~50 km from the lake and Gadara ~10 km — neither has a steep cliff into the water, prompting the Gergesa emendation. The geographical confusion is part of why critical scholarship treats the doubling as redactional rather than historical correction.

Verdict: Mark and Luke say one demoniac. Matthew doubles to two. The 'Mark omitted the second' defense is technically possible for any single case but fails as an account of the *pattern* of Matthean doublings. Held's redactional explanation is the parsimonious one.

contradictions.question: What was the name of the tax collector who was called by Jesus?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 9:9 has Jesus call a tax collector named *Maththaios* — Matthew — sitting at the customs station. Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 narrate the same scene at the same customs station with the same call-formula (*akolouthei moi* — 'follow me') and name the tax collector *Leuin* (Mark adds *ton tou Alphaiou* — 'son of Alphaeus') — Levi. Two different names for what is structurally the same call narrative.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleaner examples of how the Gospel of Matthew customizes Markan source material for its own community's purposes — and the apologist 'two names for one man' defense has to do a lot of work because there's no independent attestation that any first-century Jew named Levi was also called Matthew.

Mark 2:13-14 narrates Jesus going out by the sea, teaching the crowd, and calling *Leuin ton tou Alphaiou kathēmenon epi to telōnion* — 'Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the customs station.' Luke 5:27-28 parallels Mark almost exactly: *etheasato telōnēn onomati Leuin* — 'he observed a tax collector named Levi' — and calls him to follow.

Matthew 9:9 reproduces the same scene with one substitution: *eiden anthrōpon kathēmenon epi to telōnion, Maththaion legomenon* — 'he saw a man sitting at the customs station, called Matthew.' Same call setting, same call formula, but a different name.

The apologist harmonization — Carson, France NICNT, Bauckham *Jesus and the Eyewitnesses*, Blomberg — runs the *two-name* theory: Levi was the tax collector's birth name (Hebrew/Aramaic origin), Matthew (*Maththaios*, from Hebrew *Mattityāhū* — 'gift of YHWH') was a second name given upon discipleship-call, perhaps by Jesus himself parallel to Simon→Peter, Saul→Paul. Many first-century Jews had multiple names — a Hebrew/Aramaic name and a Greek or Latin name (cf. John Mark, Joseph Barsabbas Justus). So 'Levi the son of Alphaeus' and 'Matthew the tax collector' are the same man with two different names, and Matthew's gospel uses the man's discipleship-name because the gospel is associated with him.

That defense is non-trivial. Multiple names were common. Mark's 'Levi son of Alphaeus' (2:14) and Mark's 'James the son of Alphaeus' (3:18, in the apostle list) raise interesting questions about whether Matthew/Levi and James were brothers — though Mark doesn't make the connection. And the gospel attributed to Matthew the apostle (Matt 10:3 lists *Maththaios ho telōnēs* — 'Matthew the tax collector' — among the Twelve) would naturally want to identify the called tax collector with its own namesake.

The critical reading (Davies-Allison ICC; Luz *Hermeneia*; Marcus *AB Mark*) is that Matthew's redactor substituted 'Matthew' for Mark's 'Levi' precisely to anchor the apostle Matthew (the gospel's putative author or patron) in a call-narrative that Mark had attributed to a Levi who doesn't appear among the Twelve in any of the Synoptic apostle-lists. Levi son of Alphaeus, prominently called by Jesus in Mark 2:14, mysteriously fails to appear in Mark's own list of the Twelve in Mark 3:16-19. This is a textual problem critical scholarship has long noted: a major call-narrative figure who then disappears from the apostle-roster. Matthew's redaction solves the problem by renaming the tax collector 'Matthew,' who *is* in the Twelve list.

The two-name theory works as a logical proposition but is otherwise unsupported. There is no independent attestation that any first-century Jew was known by both 'Levi' and 'Matthew.' The Saul→Paul comparison is weak — Saul/Paul have different name-types (Hebrew vs. Roman) and are textually attested as the same person multiple times in Acts. The Simon→Peter comparison is also weak — Peter is a nickname *given by Jesus* in the gospels, narrated explicitly (Mark 3:16, John 1:42). No such renaming is narrated for Levi-becoming-Matthew. The two-name claim is an apologetic postulate created to harmonize the discrepancy.

Verdict: the two-name defense is logically possible but historically unsupported. The parsimonious critical reading is that Matthew's redactor substituted 'Matthew' for 'Levi' to anchor the apostle-Matthew tradition in the call narrative. The Levi-disappearance from Mark's own apostle list is the clue that suggests Mark's source had a non-apostle-Levi at the customs station, and Matthew's gospel adjusted the name to fit its own ecclesiastical interest.
